answer: The observed link between county food insecurity rates and diabetes hospitalizations illustrates two distinct identification problems. Bidirectional causation means hunger can worsen glucose control while illness can deepen poverty, and cross-sectional snapshots cannot tell the directions apart. Unmeasured confounding adds a second problem: poor counties have both less food access and fewer healthcare resources, so the correlation reflects shared causes rather than a clean effect. Statistical adjustment cannot resolve either issue; credible answers require study designs that supply variation in food access independent of these confounders.

faqs.q: Does food insecurity cause diabetes hospitalizations or the reverse?
faqs.a: Cross-sectional data cannot distinguish the directions. Food insecurity can impair diet and medication timing and raise hospitalizations, but chronic illness can also reduce income and increase food insecurity, so both arrows are plausible simultaneously.

faqs.q: What is the confounder in the food insecurity and diabetes case?
faqs.a: County-level poverty is a shared cause: poorer counties have both worse food access and fewer healthcare resources, less preventive care, and lower medication adherence, all of which independently raise hospitalizations.

faqs.q: Can statistical adjustment fix unmeasured confounding here?
faqs.a: No. Adjustment can only control for variables that are measured. Resolving the problem requires finding variation in food access that is independent of the confounder, typically through study design rather than regression controls.
